# To the Godly
## R E A D E R,

*And in particular to those who gladly wish to hold and attend holy private meetings <note>These were informal gatherings of believers, often called "conventicles" or "gezelschappen," held for prayer and study outside of formal church services.</note>: And most especially, to the Sanctified in the Congregation of Sluis in Flanders.*

->*Dear and Beloved in the Lord:*<-

<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter 'G' within a square frame, featuring intricate foliate designs and scrolls. Inside the curve of the 'G', there appears to be a bird-like figure.</image-desc>

Just as eight years ago I translated and brought to light for you the useful and well-crafted treatise written by a well-tested Scottish Minister, namely, *The Christian’s Great Interest*; so I bring forth to you here a no less precious treatise, written by another excellent Minister of the Church of Scotland. And I may call it, *The Second Part of the Christian’s Great Interest*, because that which was lacking in the first—namely, *using Christ for sanctification in all cases*—is here abundantly handled. Very little has been written on this subject, especially in the Netherlands; indeed, this matter is seldom handled in the pulpits, as the Ministers are often accustomed to occupy themselves with other things; although undoubtedly the foundation of this matter has been preached many times by all Ministers, yet not so clearly and distinctly. As a result, it is found that not only the common professors <term>Believers who have made a public profession of their faith</term>, but even the Godly in the land, and those who are considered the most understanding in the congregations, little understand and grasp and practice this matter—indeed, they proceed therein very darkly and confusedly; so that they can give little account of the basis and manner of their actions, or guide others in this. Nevertheless, I assure myself, and I do not doubt at all, that all tested and earnest Christians will confess and agree with me in this: That these Gospel- <note>The text ends here on a catchword; "Gospel-" (Euangeli-) likely continues as "Gospel-truths" or "Gospel-mysteries" on the following page.</note>

# To the Reader.

—the Gospel duty of using Christ intelligently for everything, and in all cases, needs, and difficulties through faith, is the fundamental duty and the mother-duty <note>The author uses "mother-duty" and "mother-grace" to describe the primary source from which all other religious obligations and virtues flow.</note> from which the others flow; just as Faith is the first grace, and the mother-grace, through which the others receive their life, activity, and power. This duty is an exercise of the Great Commandment, and it gives Christ the greatest honor, placing Him in His employment and the execution of His Offices <term>Christ's three roles as Prophet, Priest, and King</term>, and answers the Lord's objective which He has in the Gospel Covenant of Grace—namely, to be acknowledged, served, and glorified through that way of dependency and making use of the Mediator.

This duty is the nearest and most proper means to become fruitful in good works, and to grow and increase in sanctification <term>The process of being made holy</term>, and to be comforted and gladdened by the glorious riches of God’s grace. And therefore, nothing can be more desirable for those who gladly wish to please the Lord and live in close and sweet fellowship with Him—and to that end would consider it their highest happiness if they might significantly grow and increase in the mortification <note>The spiritual practice of "putting to death" sinful nature or desires.</note> of sins and the awakening of grace, walking in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit—than to receive a clear discovery of how they shall use the Fountain of all grace and comfort, and thus walk in all well-pleasing to God, bearing fruit.

How this discovery is made in this book, and how this duty and the manner of putting it well into practice is described here, I leave to you yourselves to judge and to recount when you have read the same. If you require my judgment on it, I must confess to you that I find this chief practice of a Christian described therein in an incomparably clear and concise manner, such that I have never seen or read the like on this matter. I have gladly spent my time translating this into our language, even before it was printed in the English language, so that this precious jewel—

### To the Reader.

...would become common to many; and I expect, under the Lord’s blessing, much fruit from it. Even Ministers <term>Leeraars — literally "teachers," referring to the clergy</term> will be able to derive uncommon profit from it, in order to learn to preach the Gospel purely, who now often, out of lack of understanding and inexperience, teach people to proceed in a legalistic <term>Wettische — a way focused on following the Law and human effort rather than relying on God's grace</term> manner, as they themselves frequently preach the Gospel in a legalistic way. 

But my primary objective has been to share this noble writing with the private godly souls in the Netherlands, so that those who do not hear these things publicly—or at least hear them seldom and in a more obscured way—may find them here abundantly for their instruction and refreshment. This is so that they might not remain stuck in their doubts, discouragements, and powerlessness, but that they might learn with joy to draw the Water of grace from the Fountain of salvation <note>original: "Fonteine des heils"</note>, and so run with an enlarged, lively heart on the path of God’s commandments. 

But because I know that not all are equally capable of helping themselves with books, it is my earnest request to all who are more gifted and graced, and who through this means shall be made more capable of confirming themselves and others in the course of godliness <term>Godtfaligheidt — a life of sincere piety and devotion</term> and the life of Faith, that they would do their utmost to show these thoughts and methods, indicated here, to others who are weaker, and to convey these ideas to them. This is so that the glory and riches of the Gospel, and the unsearchable Treasures of Christ <term>Schatten Christi</term>, might become better known. 

And therefore, I would wish from the heart that private holy gatherings <term>t’Samenkomsten — informal religious meetings or "conventicles" held in homes outside of official church services</term> might be held more than before. And you, who are inclined to hold and attend such meetings, I want to earnestly stir you up, so that you not only continue in them, but also attract and urge others toward them; and that neither you nor others let yourselves be deterred by the opposition which some, with a semblance of holy zeal, make against them. I speak of such gatherings...

and Gatherings, so that I may be well understood, not wherein one gossips <note>original: "achterklapt"</note> about one's neighbors, or slanders good Teachers <term>Leeraaren — ministers or clergy</term>, despises one's neighbors, speaks vainly or unedifyingly, or incites and lures others toward schism and the leaving of the Church; But where one prays with each other to the Lord, sometimes also with fasting; and where one reverently sings songs of praise to God, and Psalms, and spiritual songs, repeats and applies the preached Word, reads God's Word, and speaks of it, brings up and lays open the various experiences <term>ondervindingen — personal spiritual trials, feelings, or "dealings" with God</term> of the Pious <term>Vroome — the godly or devout</term> in the course and practice of godliness <term>Godsaligheidt — a life of sincere piety and devotion</term>, proposes, handles, and solves cases of conscience <term>gevallen van conscientie — ethical or spiritual dilemmas</term>, and useful questions about certain divine truths—those truths, and in so far as they have regard and influence on the practice of godliness; and whatever more is of such a nature, whether a Minister <term>Predikant</term> be present or not present. And to further arm You <note>original: "U. L." — short for "Uwe Liefden," an affectionate 17th-century formal address meaning "Your Loves"</note> against those who are accustomed to speak against these holy gatherings <term>t'Samenkomsten — small group meetings outside of formal church services</term> bitterly and mockingly, I would give You these reasons for the same, which now occur to me.

1. *Reason*, Because it is the Apostle's command, *Let us not neglect our mutual gatherings, but let us exhort one another*, Hebrews 10: verse 25. Thus he also makes it known there, that one should not neglect, but rather use the Christian gatherings of private Christians, for mutual conversation and the stirring up of one another; it is true, he does not exclude here the public gatherings, but includes them therein, yet that also here particularly the private gatherings are meant and intended, appears from the fact that he wants them to be observed frequently, so that one *should exhort one another*, one private Christian the other; it is then a command of God, under which all Christians lie, which they must obey for conscience's sake, whatever people may say against it.

## To the Reader.

...withdrew themselves, and made a habit of withdrawing from those Holy Gatherings <term>H. t’Samenkomsten — private religious meetings or "conventicles" held outside of formal church services</term>, saying, *Let us not do so, as some have the habit*; so then it is a notable evil to separate oneself frequently, not only from the public church Assembly, but also from the private Christian companies of the Believers <term>Geloovige</term>; and the failings of others in this regard should be so far from making us weak or negligent, that it should much rather awaken us to more diligence, to follow such a good means of edification <term>stichtingh — the process of "building up" one's faith or moral character</term>, to the end that we may give others a good example of edification in this.

3: Reason, Because observing such Holy Assemblies <term>H. Vergaderingen</term> is a means to hold fast, to confess, and not to abandon in times of trial the doctrine of Christ and the truth received and believed from Him; and on the contrary, to abandon them is the way toward division <note>original: "scheuringh" — often implying a schism or tear in the church body</note> and apostasy from the truth. For the Apostle <note>The author refers to the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews</note> prescribes this means of holding and attending mutual gatherings in order to be steadfast in the Holy Confession <term>H. Belijdenis</term>; for that was his exhortation in *verse 23: Let us hold fast the unwavering profession of hope*, and for that purpose he prescribes two means: 1. To look after one another to the sharpening and awakening of each other, *verse 24.* 2. Not to abandon or neglect the mutual gathering, *verse 25.* So that the right way to maintain unity in the Church and in the doctrine of truth is to meet together privately and frequently for mutual admonition, yet without neglect or hindrance of the public assemblies, which, as I said, are also included <note>original: "ingewonden" — literally "wrapped in" or "enwrapped," meaning these duties are inextricably linked</note>.

4. Reason, Because the day of God’s judgment <term>Godts oordeel</term>, particularly over us and generally over all, is at the door; so we should then use this means to make ourselves more fit for our duties, through which we may be in a better state on the day of our death and of our accounting; The Apostle gives this reason in the same place, saying, *Let us not [neglect] the mutual gatherings*

### To the Reader.

...abandon, and that so much the more as we see that the day approaches; He means to say, the observation of this—that there is but a short time between, and our day will have come, and our Lord will come to judgment—should serve as a suitable means and motive to sharpen you toward the observance of such an opportunity, whereby you might be confirmed and encouraged to maintain the truth against all fears of men.

5. Reason, Because Christians are commanded, in *Heb. 10: verse 24, To take heed of one another, to the sharpening of love and of good works.* Which necessarily contains within itself their fellowship with one another, and their frequent gathering with one another, and not only publicly for the open Religious Services (for then we cannot so regard one another for sharpening, since we then, and thereby, cannot see each other's condition <note>original: "gestalte" — meaning one's spiritual state or inner frame of mind</note>, gifts, virtues, etc.), but especially for private Holy Conversation <term>H. t’Samenspraak — spiritual dialogue or conference between believers</term> and interaction; for this regarding of one another consists in this: that we pay attention to one another's disposition, abilities and experiences, virtues and faults, to the end that we may make ourselves more capable of doing good to one another, and of receiving good from one another, and to stir each other up to a holy contest, as to who shall be the first in love and well-doing. Therefore, every Christian is bound to observe the Holy private Gatherings.

6. Reason, Because it is commanded of us that we should exhort one another, *Hebr. 10: verse 25.* Yea, that we should exhort one another every day, *as long as it is called Today, so that no one among us be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin, Heb. 3: verse 13.* That is, everyone must—beyond the fact that the Ministers <term>Predikanten — ordained clergy</term> exhort and awaken the Congregation <term>Gemeinte</term> publicly—speak to their fellow Christians, rouse them, and spur them on toward good, and point out to them the deceptiveness of sin, and seek to prevent the hardness of their hearts, and confirm them in the truth and steadfast...

### To the Reader.

...confession of religion, as it stands in the preceding twelfth Verse, *Take heed, Brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God*, and then follows, *But exhort one another, etc.* So this is then a necessary and general duty, which is a necessary means to keep people from apostasy <note>falling away from one's faith</note>, and a duty that must be practiced daily, while it is called Today; that is, as often and as long as God gives a present and suitable opportunity for it, so that through neglect of this, the misfortune does not follow that someone would be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. Now this duty cannot be done, if one does not speak together, and for that end gather together.

7. *Reason*, Because it is commanded that Christians should bring comforting words to one another, and speak of the lovely promises, great privileges, and glorious expectation which the Pious <note>original: "Vroome" — referring to the godly or devout believers</note> have; *So then, says the Apostle, 1 Thess. 4: verse 18. Comfort one another with these words.* Now this cannot happen unless they come together, and speak for that purpose with one another, and pray that the Lord God would bless the means, and bring the words of comfort to the hearts.

8. *Reason*, Because Christians are charged to build up, further, and edify one another's souls, as the Apostle says, *1 Thess. 5: verse 11. Wherefore exhort one another, and edify one another, even as also ye do*: This duty of edifying one another contains a great deal; each must help the other, lend a hand, strengthen, and encourage in and toward the work of the Lord. Now this is impossible to do if one only comes together in the public Assemblies <note>formal church services</note>, and then continues to live as strangers toward one another; it then necessarily follows that the Pious should frequently come together and gather for that purpose.

9. *Reason*, Because it is a general command of the Apostle, *Teach and exhort one another, and speak among...*

### To the Reader.

*...one another with Psalms, and Hymns, and spiritual Songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with grace in your heart*, Col. 3: verse 16. Eph. 5: verse 19. No one can think that this can happen, unless for that purpose people gather together outside of the public Assemblies.

10. *Reason*, Because it flows from the nature of the Christian communion of the Saints <note>The "communion of saints" is a core doctrine in the Apostles' Creed, referring to the spiritual union and mutual service of all believers</note>, which everyone professes to believe; now that communion requires and contains, among other things, a communal sharing of gifts and graces, for the improvement, enlightenment, awakening, and strengthening of one another, which our Catechism <note>Refers to the Heidelberg Catechism, a standard Protestant instructional document used in the Dutch Reformed Church</note> expresses thus in the 55th *Question*, saying, that *everyone, by virtue of the communion of the Saints, must know himself bound to employ his gifts for the use and salvation of the other members, willingly and with joy*; Thus these Holy private Gatherings and meetings must be held, or the communion of the Saints will be denied in practice, and the Catechism contradicted; for how can that sharing and employing of talents for others happen, without often coming together?

11. *Reason*, Because it is commanded, that *one shall confess sins to one another, and pray for one another*, James 5: verse 16. So then one must come to the other, and speak of the matters of the Soul, and be together in prayer, not only in public Assemblies, but privately, private Christians with one another; the more so because the Pattern of prayers <note>The Lord's Prayer</note> shows us that the Believers must frequently worship their heavenly Father in unison, saying, *Our Father*, etc.

12. *Reason*, Because every Believer must conduct himself as a Distributor <note>original: "Uitdeelder" — meaning a steward or someone who dispenses God's grace to others</note>, and not as an Owner and Master of his gifts; since God has given everyone gifts out of grace, for a common use, for the edification of others, according to the encouragement and the charge of the Apostle Peter, 1 Pet. 4: 10. *As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God*; Everyone must put his talent to use <note>original: "op woeker" — literally "at interest," referring to the Parable of the Talents where servants are expected to grow what was entrusted to them</note>

### To the Reader.

...to put <note>Completing the thought from the previous page: "to put [one's talents] to work"</note> to use, seeking to gain profit for his Lord and Master, laboring to catch souls and win them for Christ, and to convert sinners from the error of their ways and save them from death: everyone, having been converted, must also strengthen his brother; everyone must employ the gifts according to the grace given to him, according to *Matt. 25: verses 26, 27; Prov. 11: verse 30; James 5: verse 20; Luke 22: verse 32; Rom. 12: verses 6, 7; 1 Cor. 12: verse 7.* This indicates that it is the Lord's will and pleasure that Christians should hold mutual meetings frequently and on all good occasions.

13. *Reason*, Because the need of Christians requires that they be together frequently, since they have need of one another for help, encouragement, and support; no Christian can so exist on his own that he does not need his neighbor: they must join together, and each fulfill the other's need, and strengthen and support one another’s hands. *Two are better than one, says the Preacher <note>Referring to the author of the book of Ecclesiastes</note>: because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up. And if one prevail against him, then two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken. Eccl. 4: verses 9, 10, 12.* The members of the mystical Body of Christ <note>A theological concept describing the spiritual unity of all believers with Jesus as the "head"</note> need each other and must have the same care for one another: *the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee; the members which seem to be more feeble are necessary, 1 Cor. 12: verses 21, 22, 25.* The <term>spiritual experiences</term> <note>original: "bevindingen" – a central term in Dutch Pietism referring to the internal, lived reality of faith and God's work in the soul</note>, deliverances, and comforts of one are useful for the other. Paul, an Apostle, not only needed the prayers of the believers in Rome, but also the comfort and strengthening through their faith, and for that reason he longed to see them and come to them, *Rom. 15: verse 30; Rom. 1: verses 11, 12, 13.* and in general the Apostle says to the believers...

...all be subject to one another, and that in the fear of God, *1 Peter 5: verse 5; Ephesians 5: verse 21.* And therefore serve one another, and rebuke and receive rebukes from the other; how would this happen, if we did not more often come together?

17. **Reason**, Because Christians, as Brothers and Sisters, Housemates, and Children of one Father, must maintain friendship; they are very closely related and must treat one another with fervent brotherly love, and be kind, as Peter says, *1 Peter 3: verse 8.* So they must come together more often, and visit one another, and speak and write to one another, and associate with one another as intimate Friends (just as the Virgin *Mary* visited her cousin *Elizabeth* for that purpose, *Luke 1: 39-57*) quite differently than they associate with godless worldly people. In the public Gatherings the Godless and the Pious are mixed together, except in the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Avontmaal"; referring to Holy Communion, where traditionally only the faithful were admitted</note>, where only Friends are commanded to eat; therefore other opportunities should be seized, in which they, as one heart and soul, would practice friendship together. It is known that the nature of honest friendship requires social interaction, visiting, conversation, sharing, and hospitality; for its definition is that it is a mutual goodwill which one does not allow to remain hidden. Shall then Christian and Godly friendship not much more have these expressions within it, and require the company and inward fellowship of one with another? Would they then not receive and embrace one another with affection according to the Apostle’s lesson, *Romans 15: verse 7: Receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.*

18. **Reason**, Because it is the Lord’s commandment that people be of one mind, and speak with one language concerning the Holy truth and Godliness; Paul prayed for the Romans thus: *Now the God of patience and consolation grant you to be likeminded one toward another according to Christ* <meta>catchword: Iesum [Jesus]</meta>

Experience teaches this abundantly, so much so that the enemies of these gatherings and exercises <note>The term "exercises" (Dutch: *oeffeningen*) refers to informal religious meetings where laypeople discussed scripture and shared spiritual experiences.</note> are accustomed to object, among other things, that people become "too wise," or "know-it-alls" <note>Original: *neuswijs*. Furthermore, many are converted through this means; indeed, it is experienced in some places that where these exercises are maintained with earnestness, zeal, and spiritual composure, more souls are converted than are observed to be touched by public preaching <note>Formal sermons delivered by a minister during a church service.</note>. Many a soul has felt the first breathings and stirrings of God's Spirit there; there their eyes were first opened, so that they saw that Christianity was something other than mere confession <note>Publicly stating one's faith or adherence to a creed.</note>, church-going, and civic morality. They found there that the doctrine of the Holy Gospel had brought forth a wonderful change and new life in some people; so that through those exercises, they have come not only to a healthy suspicion of themselves and their own spiritual state, but also to the beginnings of spiritual life and renewal. Through this, many have advanced in the art and skill of praying; people who previously might have had enough grace to sigh somewhat to God according to their need, but from hearing the exercise...

Is it any wonder that such people seek help and counsel and guidance from one another, since they know that the great mass of Professors <note>original: "Belijders"; here referring to those who claim faith in name only</note> deceive themselves with delusions and will remain outside of Heaven, and that they themselves have a deceitful and deadly heart, just like others, and that they as well as others have their temptations and obstacles from within and without? It seems to me rather a great wonder that Christians—who together as travelers and strangers on earth and Citizens of Heaven set their course heavenward, and fight the same fight to be crowned, and carry on the same heavenly business—could be occupied in any other business, or in any other company where one speaks of earthly trifles.

Thus we are bound all the more to attend and maintain those private gatherings of the faithful, being fully assured that those who oppose and rail against these assemblies strive, in fact, against Christ and against his laws, and against obedience to his commands—as is clearly to be inferred from the reasons set forth above. The very learned and godly Master **Gisbertus Voetius** <term>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676): A hugely influential Dutch Reformed theologian and lead figure of the "Further Reformation," known for emphasizing personal piety alongside strict doctrine</term>, presenting to himself that objection:

*Suppose that those mutual visits of godliness—those gatherings and conversations—were forbidden somewhere; it would not follow from that that they are unlawful in the Court of Heaven or of the Conscience. For such a penal law would no more bind the consciences of the believers than the Ordinances of **Darius** <note>original: "Dan. 6"; refers to the biblical story of Daniel continuing to pray despite the King's decree</note>, and of the Great Council <note>original: "Hand. 4. en 5."; refers to Acts of the Apostles chapters 4 and 5, where the Apostles tell the authorities they must obey God rather than men</note>, and of the Roman Emperors against the Christians, and of **Charles the Fifth** and **Philip the Second** <note>The Spanish monarchs who ruled the Netherlands and persecuted Protestants during the 16th century</note> in the year 1563, and of other Princes against the Reformed.*

We must show through our actions that we desire to obey the command of God in this matter, and follow the counsel and the example of the pious, to the shaming of the world and the stopping of the mouths of the slanderers. A pious **Teacher** in the Netherlands wrote not long ago concerning this:

*Those meetings of the godly, for mutual exhortation, instruction, and comfort, were instituted by the Lord as auxiliary means to further our inward service which we owe to Him; they have always been praised by the Saints and practiced at all times. Thus it demonstrates itself that it is not only lawful, but also highly commendable to arrange the same occasionally, and to attend them with a humble and studious heart.*

These gatherings, he says, of the Christians were rightly to be considered unlawful if they were like illicit meetings; they were rightly to be condemned if they could be accused under the name and heading of Factions or conspiracies; but to whose ruin have we ever come together? We are the same, whether we are gathered or scattered, whether we are together or alone; we wrong no one, we grieve no one. Whenever the Pious and Good come together, whenever the Godly and Chaste assemble, then it must not be called a conspiracy, but a Council or a Court.

...suffering persecution, being cast out by force by the High Powers of this Land from my congregation, because of my opposition to the Service of the Liturgy <term>Formulier-dienst: The mandatory use of prescribed liturgical forms or prayer books, which some reformed ministers resisted as an infringement on spiritual freedom.</term> and the observance of Feast Days, and the usurping of ecclesiastical power by the Civil Magistrates <term>Politijken: Secular authorities or 'politicians' who claimed jurisdiction over church affairs, a major point of contention during the Dutch Reformation.</term>; and being hindered by the Ministers, my fellow-servants, from publicly preaching the Gospel, which they well know is entrusted to me as much as to them. Indeed, the height of the perversity of the Ministers goes so far in some places that they even dare to use the secular Arm <note>original: "wereltlijken Arm"; this refers to the use of state police or military force to enforce religious compliance.</note> to violently prevent that preaching of the Gospel by one who they must admit has a calling and commission from Christ for that purpose. How they shall answer for that before the Lord Jesus, I leave for you to consider; and at the same time, to judge from this how fallen and miserable the state of the Church of the Netherlands is, when even those who have a reputation for being alive and well-meaning are so far led astray.

But upon you, *my very beloved and dear Friends*, sanctified in the Congregation of *Sluis in Flanders*, I have had my eye most especially in bringing this book to light. For your edification has been particularly laid upon me, and you lie very near to my heart because of the good that the Lord has done for you under my ministry. I have indeed been separated from you by force, but I cannot, I may not rest from bringing you all possible help according to my ability and opportunity. Therefore, I send you this excellent book. I know you expect something of my own making, but as I am certain that I could not make it as well as this, I now give this to you much rather; and you may receive it with no less affection. I have preached to you much about these and similar matters, as you will remember, and have tried to teach you, publicly and privately, how Christ is to be used through faith in all necessities—which I also, by the Lord’s blessing, have found that many have grasped so well that they have successfully overcome many obstacles and difficulties, which the

## To the Reader:

...tend to hold back the comfort and the strength of Christians for a long time; this book shall be of further help to you in this, for which I pray to the Lord, and shall continue to pray. You all now miss my ministry for a time, and you suffer this violence along with me and sigh over it; but the Lord hears it, and sees it, and shall answer in His own time and way. Yet I assure you that, just as God is mighty to make all Grace <term>Genade: The unmerited favor of God, a central concept in Reformed theology where salvation is a gift rather than something earned.</term> abound in you, so that you, having all sufficiency in all things at all times, may abound in every good work, He shall likewise faithfully satisfy your souls with good things, even with the fatness of His house; for He is faithful who has promised, provided that you, in the evangelical way, by virtue of the Covenant of Grace <term>Verbondt der genade: The theological framework describing God's promise of eternal life through faith in Christ, contrasting with a 'Covenant of Works'.</term>, through faith, draw all comfort and strength from the Mediator <term>Middelaar: A title for Jesus Christ, acting as the legal and spiritual intermediary between God and humanity.</term>. Now I find that when I begin to speak to you, my heart is very ready to write many things for your exhortation and warning; yet because I have perhaps already overstepped the bounds of a preface, I must restrain myself and postpone that until another occasion. *I shall mention only two things* about which I now wish to exhort you. *The first is, that you*, in your receiving of Christ as your Lord and King, might act so wisely that you do not fall short of the evangelical design of our God in this—that is, that you look upon and embrace Jesus' Kingly Office <term>Koninklijk Ampt: Christ's role as the sovereign ruler over the believer's life and the church, providing protection and governance.</term> as much for healing as you do His Priestly Office <term>Priester-Ampt: Christ's role in offering Himself as a sacrifice for sins and interceding with God on behalf of believers.</term>. It is a mistake that many Christians so receive Jesus as Lord and King that they only consent to Him in order to serve and obey Him, so that they only think that Jesus as King is received...

### To the Reader.

...must [offer him] honor and obedience, as being the Lawgiver and commander, who is worthy—on account of His work as High Priest—that we dedicate all the powers of our soul to him, and devote everything to his service. Yet certainly this is a great and harmful misunderstanding; it is as if Jesus had only become King for himself and for his own honor, and not for the good of his dearly-bought children. Or, if one takes the idea a bit further, it is as if He, as King, only had to protect his subjects against the Devil and the world, and thereafter receive from them obedience out of gratitude for the redemption obtained through his Blood. 

But this is a legalistic <term>Wettisch: Referring to a 'Covenant of Works' mindset where one tries to earn God’s favor through law-keeping, rather than receiving it through faith.</term> conception of Christ’s Kingly Office <term>Koninklijk Ampt: One of the three roles of Christ (Prophet, Priest, and King) in Reformed theology; here specifically focusing on His power to rule over the believer's heart.</term>, through which we act in a legalistic and slavish manner—as if we were outside a Covenant of Grace <term>Verbondt der Genade: God’s promise of salvation through faith in Christ’s merits rather than the believer's own efforts.</term> with him in this matter. In such a state, we often find the heart disinclined to accept him under that consideration, because we find ourselves very unwilling and unable to obey his holy commands. Indeed, we find the heart rebellious, averse, loathing, and ready to run away from the Lord Jesus. Thus, we not only derive no comfort from our acceptance of him as King, but we receive from it a great wound and a shaking of our faith and trust. For we must accept Christ very willingly in his three Offices <note>The "three offices" (Latin: *munus triplex*) are Prophet, Priest, and King.</note>, and when this does not align with our desires—as is truly the case with a hypocrite—we are then ready to call all our graces and our entire spiritual state into doubt. 

That mistake you must then correct, and you shall have much comfort and refreshment from it, and Christ shall have all the more honor from it. Namely: you must accept him as King in such a way that you permit him to effectively, powerfully, and with a spiritual and lovely violence <note>Original: "lieffelijk gewelt." A common phrase in 17th-century Dutch piety referring to the "sweet" way God’s grace overpowers a rebellious human will without coercing it against its ultimate interest.</note> install himself as King. This should happen not only in your first turning to him, but continually in the exercise of your faith regarding him. You must take him into your heart as one who is both coming and willing to subject your heart and inclinations to himself, and to kill and break the spiritual enemies within your soul—yes, in order to...

# To the Reader.

[...but] to root out your enmity, which you still have against him because of the remnants of sin, through his Spirit; as he was made King for that purpose in grace over us, to kill the foreign lords <note>The "foreign lords" refers to sinful desires, passions, or spiritual idols that rule the human heart in place of God.</note> within us, and as an all-conquering and overpowering King, to make everything subject and obedient to himself; as a King, he comes to heal the breach on our side, to bend our hearts toward willing obedience and the practical execution of his will; and in this respect, for a sincere Soul—however weak it may be, and however much it finds the **body of sin** <note>original: "Lichaam der zonde." A biblical term (Romans 6:6) referring to the corrupt human nature that persists even after a person begins their spiritual life.</note> stirring within itself—Christ’s **Kingly Office** shall be as dear and desirable and worthy of longing as his **Priestly Office**, and that soul will shrink as little from embracing Jesus as King as it shrinks from embracing him as Priest; and surely this is a most precious thought, which is of great value to us; especially to answer our objections that flow from the power of sin remaining within us.

We find ourselves greatly refreshed when many objections occur to us, arising from our heavy debt of sin, in that we can look to Jesus as a **High Priest**, who through his bloody atoning sacrifice <note>original: "zoen-offer." This refers to the propitiation or satisfaction of God's justice through the death of Christ, which removes the legal "debt" of sin.</note> (all-sufficient and infinitely worthy for the removal of the debt of sin) has made peace and **reconciliation**, and that we may freely—indeed, must in every way—accept him, as it is commanded of us; but concerning the *power* of sin within us, we find more difficulty. Yet the Lord be praised, that has been provided for just as well as the removal of the guilt; for we may and must look to Jesus as a King and exalted Prince, who can, will, and shall—and by virtue of his office <term>Ampt: A formal duty or role (Prophet, Priest, or King) that Christ is divinely commissioned by God to fulfill for the sake of the church.</term> must—subdue and conquer our and his spiritual enemies in us and for us, and we only have to consent to him and call upon him as such a King, given to us by the Father, and placed upon the throne to carry this out; Christ sits on his Priestly Throne to make reconciliation on God’s side, and on his Kingly throne, to [all...]

# To the Reader.

...what is in us to bow to his willing obedience, which the Prophet expresses thus: *Behold, a man whose name is the Branch; he shall build the Temple of the Lord, and he shall bear the glory, and he shall sit and rule upon his throne, and he shall be a Priest upon his throne, Zech. 6:12, 13.* <note>The "Branch" (Dutch: *Spruite*) is a Messianic title from the Old Testament, representing Christ as the descendant of David who restores the temple.</note> The Lord Jesus is exalted as a Prince, to give repentance and forgiveness, *Acts 5: verse 31.* He has come to powerfully break the works of the Devil in us, *1 John 3: verse 8,* and to draw us out of this present evil world, *Gal. 1: verse 4,* and to redeem us from our vain conduct <note>original: "ydele vvandeling." Secondly, regarding the Gatherings <note>original: "t'Samenkomften." Thus I shall end, praying, as Paul did for those of Colossae, that you might *be filled with the knowledge of God's will, in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of the Lord, unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God; strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joy.*

# JESUS All in All.

->Tune: *Our Father.*<- <note>original: "Stemme. Onze Vader." Referring to the standard melody used for the Lord's Prayer in Reformed liturgy.</note>

1. O Jesus, make the delusion of being "something"
In me, completely and utterly, into nothing.
And be alone henceforth *All in All,*
What I am, and what I shall be.
Let all that is old pass away,
And make *everything new* in me.

2. What does it benefit me, if I know everything,
If I am ignorant of you?
What does it harm me, if I knew nothing,
If only I know you, o *Christ!*
O only pledge worthy of being known;
Be *All in All my understanding.*

3. The <term>Triangle</term> <note>A common 17th-century emblem: the human heart was depicted as a triangle (representing the Trinity or the heart's three corners) which cannot be filled by the "circle" of the world, but only by God.</note> of my eager heart,
Is never filled by the <term>all-encompassing world.</term> <note>original: "’t All-rondt," referring to the physical globe or the circularity of worldly vanities.</note>
My hope, and fear, and joy, and desire,
And love never find rest.
Be *All*, Lord, as the occasion requires,
In *all my affections.*

4. As the man is, so is his strength: <note>A reference to Judges 8:21.</note>
But I am nothing, and my power is nothing.
My enemies are many and evil,
Their schemes are strong, their strength is hollow.
So that I do not come to a fall,
Be, Lord, *my entire suit of armor.* <note>original: "mijn Wapen-rusting All," referencing the "Armor of God" from Ephesians 6.</note>

5. Away with profit, pleasure, status, and honor,
I want you as my only goal;
Whether I eat, or whether I drink,
Or whether I do any other thing;
All that I think, or speak, or work,
Be *All*, Lord, in my focus.

6. The friendship of this world is evil,
In enmity and hatred against God,
So that I henceforth am no friend of it;
Nor know Father or Mother,
Except those who are also of your number;
Be, Lord, in all my friendship, all.

## CHAPTER I.
### The Introduction, with some general observations from the context. <note>The "context" (original: "aan-een-hang") refers to how these specific verses relate to the passages surrounding them in the Bible.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'H' featuring elaborate foliate designs within a square border.</image-desc>

IT is undoubtedly always useful, indeed necessary, for the children of God to know the proper way to make use of Christ, who has become everything to them that they need; namely wisdom, <term>righteousness</term> <note>The state of being right or justified before God.</note>, <term>sanctification</term>, and <term>redemption</term> <note>Deliverance from sin and its consequences.</note>: 1 Corinthians 1:30. But it is never more necessary for believers to know how to act clearly and discerningly in this matter than when <term>Satan</term> seeks by all means to pervert the straight ways of the Lord, and in one way or another to lead souls away—

# Christus the Way,
<meta>catchword: from</meta>

from and to draw [them] away from *Christ*, knowing full well that if he prevails here, he has won his case. And there he seeks not only to obscure the Truth through error <note>original: "dwaling"</note>, be it coarser or finer, but also to obscure it through misconceptions and prejudices; from which it happens that not only strangers come to wander off from the Way, but also frequently many of God’s own People come to walk in darkness of ignorance and misconceptions, and remain meager for lack of the actual exercise of the Life of Faith. This exercise would otherwise make them healthy and flourishing, because it would make them strong in the Lord, and in the strength of His power, and would cause them to grow up in *Christ* in all things.

The laying open then of this Truth can be nothing other than very timely now, when *Satan* prevails over many—those whom he cannot entice to looseness and profanity—to sit down upon something that is not *Christ*, and to rest upon something that is within themselves, which is distinct from Him, both in the matter of <term>justification</term> <note>Being declared righteous before God.</note> and of <term>sanctification</term> <note>The process of growing in holiness.</note>. But if He, on account of sin, should hide Himself and not send forth these rays of light through which we might discover light, then we shall only darken counsel with words without knowledge, and leave the matter as unclear as it ever was.

Therefore it is necessary that there be—both in him who writes and in those who read—a simple dependence upon Him who is given as a Leader (Isaiah 55: verse 4) and has promised to lead the blind by the Way they have not known, and to make them walk through the paths they have not known, and to make the darkness before their face into light, and the crooked into straight (Isaiah 42: verse 16). So that we, thus exercising faith in Him, might find the truth of this verified—namely, that He is the *Way*, the *Truth*, and the *Life*.

# The Truth and the Life.

[He] takes <note>the opportunity</note> to further explain that foundation of comfort to them, and to make them see the true way to come to the Father, so that they might be helped by it to see that they were not such strangers to the way as they thought they were. He does this in such a manner that they might simultaneously see that the Way is perfect, full, safe, saving, and sufficient, and also learn their duty to use this way always and in everything, until they finally come home to the Father, saying:

> *I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life: No one comes to the Father except through me.*

When *Christ* says then, that He is not only the Way to the Father—namely the true and living Way—but that He is so much the true Way that He is also the Truth itself, in the abstract <note>original: "in het afgetrokkene"; meaning in His very essence or absolute nature</note>, and that He is such a living Way that He is the Life itself in the abstract, He gives us a foundation to notice in what manner He is the Truth and the Life as well as the Way. This serves to clarify and reveal that He is an absolutely perfect, surpassingly excellent, incomparably desirable, and fully satisfying Way—useful for the believer in all cases, in all needs, in all miseries, in all difficulties, in all trials, in all temptations, in all doubts, in all anxieties, and in all causes or occasions of spiritual imbalances <note>original: "ongetempertheden"; refers to a lack of inner peace or emotional/spiritual instability</note>, fears, faintings, discouragements, etc., which they might encounter on their way to Heaven.

-># the Truth, and the Life.<-

his lack of tenderness and compassion; but further.

Secondly, we see that weaknesses and corruptions <note>The Dutch "verdorventheden" refers to the inherent flaws or "corruptions" of human nature in a theological sense.</note> breaking out in the believer, when they are sincerely and simply laid before the Lord, will not drive Him away, but will bind Him all the more to help and stand by them. Much of the weakness and corruption of *Thomas* appeared in what he said; nevertheless, when these were sincerely and simply placed before *Christ*—not out of a spirit of contradiction, but out of a desire to learn—*Christ* is so far from pushing him away that He much more inclines Himself, out of love and tenderness of heart, to instruct him better and to lay open the way more perfectly. And that for two reasons: 1. Because He well knows our frame and fashion, how insignificant and fragile we are, and that if He were to deal with us according to our folly, we would quickly be destroyed. 2. He is not as *men* are—hasty, frivolous, or proud—but kind, loving, tender, and full of compassion. It is His office and His own work to be a teacher of the ignorant, a helper of our weaknesses and fragilities, and a *Physician* <note>original: "Medicijnmeester," literally a "Medicine-master" or master healer.</note> to bind up and heal our sores and wounds.

But what are these false and deceitful ways in which people exhaust themselves, all in vain? Which ways do they choose and trust in, even though they are not the way that will be found safe and secure?

I answer: it would not be easy to list them all. We shall mention some of the most prominent and common ones, namely:

1. **Good intentions and resolutions**, with which many deceive themselves, thinking that such is all that is required. Alas, all their intentions are like Ephraim’s goodness: like the morning cloud and the early dew that vanishes quickly. <note>The author references Hosea 6:4, comparing fleeting faith to morning mist.</note> Their intentions are soon broken off and nullified because they are made without counsel, *Proverbs 15: verse 22.* Many foolishly rest in the fact that they have a "good mind" to do better and to improve their ways; they plan that after this or that time, they will begin a new way of life. 2. **Certain convictions and internal accusations**; the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Bible or the preaching of Scripture.</note> occasionally pierces so deep, and heavy and sharp visitations <note>A "visitation" from the Lord usually refers to a period of divine testing, judgment, or trial intended to wake the conscience.</note> from the Lord affect their hearts so much that they see things are not right with them. <meta>This page transitions from the general necessity of a Mediator to a specific four-part examination of Christ as "the Way." # Christ the Way,

given among men, whereby we must be saved. <note>Acts 4: v. 12.</note>

To explain this clearly, we shall speak briefly of these four things and show:

**First, what our state is, and how much we need a way.**

**Secondly, how *Christ* answers this state of ours, and is a suitable way for us.**

**Thirdly, how He alone is this way, and satisfies our case.**

**Fourthly, what the uncommon advantages and particulars of this way are.**

And this shall pave the way, so that we may clearly show how *Christ* must be used as a path by poor sinners.

Regarding the first matter, namely our present case and need, something has been spoken of this previously. We shall bring everything under these two headings. The first is our state of guilt and separation from God, due to sin and guilt. The other is our state of godlessness and enmity against God.

Regarding the first, we may take notice of these things:

1. ### the Truth, and the Life.

# Christ the Way,

### treatise—namely, *The Christian’s Great Interest*; 

so shall we come and show how a believer, or a justified soul, shall further use *Christ* for sanctification <note>The lifelong process of becoming more holy and Christ-like in character and behavior.</note>, since this is a particular matter regarding which she <note>The "soul" is traditionally referred to with feminine pronouns in this period's theological writing.</note> is often very perplexed and burdened.

In order that we might, to some extent through the help of His light and grace, present some things to clear up this great and necessary truth, we shall first speak of it in general, and then proceed to show the matter more particularly. Before we speak of the matter in general, we ought to remember that the *Person* who alone is in a state to use *Christ* for sanctification is one who has already used *Christ* for righteousness and justification <note>The legal act where God declares a sinner righteous through faith in Christ.</note>. He who is a stranger to *Christ* and still lives in a natural state has no access to *Christ* for sanctification. He must be a believer and be in the covenant <note>Referring to the Covenant of Grace, a core Reformed theology concept describing God's promise of eternal life through faith.</note> before he can make use of the grounds of sanctification presented in the covenant; one must first be united with *Christ* and justified through faith in him before one can draw any power from him for the perfecting of holiness. He must first be in him before he can grow in him, or bring forth fruit in him. And therefore, the first thing with which souls should occupy themselves is how to be united with *Christ* and clothed with his righteousness through faith; and then they have a right to all his benefits. First, they should seek to have their state changed from enmity to peace and reconciliation with *God* through faith in *Jesus*.

But on the other hand, one should note that when it is said that one must be a believer before one can go to *Christ* and use him for holiness and purification, it is not understood nor said that one must *know* for certain that they are already justified through faith before they can make any use of *Christ* for sanctification.

thus to cast himself, and his care and burden upon Him who cares for him. <note>1 Peter 5:7, Psalm 37:5, Psalm 55:22</note> In this way the work would become light and certain, as we through faith roll the burden upon Him who is the Chosen One, made fit for that work; and leave it to Him, who is our strength, patiently awaiting the outcome in hope.

In this manner the believer makes use of Christ, as having been made by God for sanctification, <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:30: "Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification."</note> when in the use of the established means—looking to the Covenant of grace and its promises, and to what Christ has done to sanctify and purify His people—he rolls the matter upon Him and expects help, salvation, and victory through Him.

But lest some should become faint-hearted, and think that all is in vain because they nevertheless perceive no progress or growth in grace, but find corruption to be as strong and troublesome as ever, I wish to say a few things to them.

**First.** Let them examine and test whether their shortcoming and failure in expectation does not largely arise because the matter was not cast so purely upon Christ as it ought to have been. Is it not too often found that they go out to battle in their own strength, leaning on their own capital <note>original: "capitaal"; referring to one's own internal stock or accumulated reserves of spiritual strength</note> of grace, on their own knowledge, or on their duties, or the like? How then can they be successful?

**Secondly.** Let them mourn when they receive any discovery of this, and arm themselves hereafter against that corrupt inclination of the heart which continually prompts them to engage in the battle without the Captain <note>original: "Oversten"; can also mean Chief, Prince, or Commander</note> of their salvation, and to fight without the armor of God.

**Thirdly.** Let them test and see whether, in striving for holiness, they are not led by wrong ends, and whether they do not seek sanctification more so that they may be worthier and better accepted by God,

### CHAPTER VI.

## How *Christ* is to be used, in respect of the killing and crucifying of the Old Man.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' featuring floral and vine motifs within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

Having thus briefly pointed out some things in general / serving to explain and open the way / how *Christ* is to be used for <term>sanctification</term> <note>original: "heilighmakingh"; the process of being made holy.</note> / we now come / to lay this work open more particularly. In sanctification we must first observe the renewal and change of our nature / and form. Secondly, the washing and cleansing of our daily acquired stains. The first of these is commonly divided into two parts, namely the killing, <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "mortificatie"; from the Latin 'mortificatio', referring to the spiritual practice of "putting to death" sinful desires.</note> / and crucifying of the <term>old man</term> <note>original: "ouden mensch"; a biblical term for the human nature corrupted by sin.</note> of sin / and of the corruption / that is within us; and the <term>quickening</term> <note>original: "levendigmaking"; bringing to life.</note>, renewal / awakening / and strengthening of the <term>new man</term> <note>original: "nieuwen mensch"; the nature of a believer transformed by grace.</note> of grace; And this is a growth in grace / and in fruitfulness / and holiness.

As concerns the first of these / namely / the Mortification, or crucifying of the Old Man / we ought to know / that there is now / since the <term>Fall</term> <note>original: "val"; the theological event of humanity's first sin in Eden.</note> / such a principle of wickedness and enmity against God in man / through which man is inclined to evil / and only toward evil. This is called the Old Man / being as it were a body / made up of so many parts / joints / and members / that is / so many lusts / and corruptions / and evil inclinations / which together make up a *body* <note>original: "corpus"</note> / and are firmly united / and bound together / just like the members of the body / each useful and of service to the other / and all these working together / and contributing their best

guard himself against this enemy, to have a watchful eye

The old man <note>The "old man" is a biblical term referring to the unregenerate human nature before spiritual transformation.</note> with his deeds ought to be put to death, Colossians 3: verse 9, and we must kill our members which are on the earth, verse 5: for all these are against us, and the least of them favored, entertained, and embraced will work our ruin and murder our soul; therefore the believer ought to look upon each one of them, and upon them all, as his deadly enemies.

Thirdly. He ought to consider that just as it is a very unseemly thing for him to be a slave of that old Tyrant, and to present his members as so many servants of unrighteousness; it is also dangerous and deadly; his life depends on it; either he must get sin mortified <term>mortified: from the Latin 'mortificatio', meaning the putting to death or subduing of sinful desires through spiritual discipline</term>, killed, and brought under subjection, or it will kill him: his life shall have to go for the life of sin; if this enemy escapes, he is a lost man. The consideration of this ought to make the believer set to work here with earnestness and diligence, with care and industriousness, and to undertake this work of mortification with labor and effort.

That law of sin and of death which rules over a **Man** who still lives in nature—and is not yet planted by faith into the likeness of His death, nor buried with Him through **Baptism** into death, *Rom. 6: verse 4, 5*—has no dominion over the believer such as it once had. For the law of the **Spirit** of life in **Christ Jesus** has made her free from the law of sin and of death, *Rom. 8: verse 2*, so that the believer is now free from that tyranny. That tyrant can now exercise no legal jurisdiction or authority over him, and therefore he may repel the insolence of that tyrant with even greater courage—one who, against all right and fairness, still seeks to hold dominion over him. He is no legal subject of that cruel and raging **Prince**, or of that spiritual wickedness.

## Objections answered.

It will not be in vain, for the further opening of the matter, to remove a scruple <note>a "scrupel" here refers to a lingering doubt or a troubled conscience</note> or two. Some might say that they cannot notice that all their trouble in this has any good outcome: for never did they find their **corruption** stir itself more, or work more vigorously and constantly, than since they began in earnest to fight against it; so that this would seem not to be the right way.

I Answer: Although a solution to this doubt can be obtained from what was said before, particularly from the ninth and thirteenth warnings, I will nevertheless present these things for further clarification of the matter.

1. Could not much of this flow from the fact that you do not take the whole work away from yourself and lay it upon **Christ**, as you ought to do? Test yourself, and see.

2. Can the **Devil** not rage the most when he thinks he will shortly be cast out? Can he not labor to cause the soul the most trouble when he sees that he will certainly be evicted from some of his strongholds?

3. Can the **Devil** not do this intentionally to drive the soul to despair of ever getting **corruption** brought under and killed; or to a faint—

to which we are called by God, yet it is beyond our hand and power. It is true: in conversion <term>bekeering: the spiritual turning point where a person is brought to faith</term> the seed of grace is cast into the soul, new habits <term>heblijkheden: from the Latin 'habitus,' referring to infused spiritual qualities or dispositions of the soul</term> are poured in, a new principle of life is given, and the heart of stone is changed into a heart of flesh; nonetheless, these principles and habits cannot work of themselves, nor be brought into activity by anything that a believer—considered in himself and without Divine help—can do.

For the smallest sin cannot be forgiven except through **Jesus Christ**: for **God’s** Law is violated by it, His justice provoked, **God’s** authority held in low regard, etc. And therefore it cannot now be forgiven because of the threats tied to the transgression of the Law, without a ransom <note>original: "rantzoen" — a theological term for the price paid by Christ to satisfy divine justice</note>. Death is the wage of all sin, smaller and greater; and the curse applies to all sinners, greater and smaller. Therefore, a believer should not allow any sin, once seen and noticed, to lie unforgiven; but upon its first discovery, he should go and bring it to **Christ** and nail it to His cross.

**Tenthly**, The believer should not conclude that his sins are not forgiven because perhaps temporal plagues <note>original: "tijdelijke plagen" — meaning earthly hardships or disciplinary consequences in this life, as opposed to eternal punishment</note>, imposed because of those sins, have not been removed. For although **David’s** sin was forgiven, nevertheless, because of that sin of his, a temporal plague lay upon him and upon his house until his dying day. For not only did **God** take that child away through death, 2 Samuel 12: <margin>verse 14.</margin> but He said to him that the sword would never depart from his house, and that He would stir up evil against him out of his own house, and give his wives to one who would lie with them in the sight of the sun, <margin>verses 10, 11.</margin> so we read that the **Lord** took vengeance on their deeds, whose sins He had forgiven, Psalm 99: <margin>verse 8.</margin> **God** can judge this to be fitting and useful for His own honor, and for their humiliation, and to make them fear sinning against Him all the more. Indeed, not only can temporal plagues be imposed because of sin that is forgiven; but even the feeling of **God’s** wrath can last after forgiveness, as is evident from that Penitential Psalm <note>original: "boet-Psalm" — one of several psalms used to express deep repentance, specifically referring here to the famous "Miserere"</note>, Psalm 51, written by **David** after **Nathan** had spoken to him regarding his sin.

I Answer: This very same way must be followed there as well. There is such a thing as an **implicit repentance** <note>original: "ingewikkelde bekeeringh" — a general turning away from sin that covers all faults, even those the believer does not specifically recognize at the moment</note> for sins that have not been distinctly seen or noticed. In the same way, an **implicit faith** can be at work; that is, the believer, being convinced that he is guilty of more sins than those he has yet gained a clear sight of, just as he must lament his state before **God** on account of these sins and exercise a godly sorrow over them, so he ought to take them as if in a heap, or as if in a **sealed bundle**, and nail them by faith to the cross of **Christ**, as if they had all been distinctly seen and known. *Who can understand his errors?* said **David**, **Psalm 19: verse 12** <note>original: "vers 13" — in older Dutch Bibles, the numbering of Psalms often differs by one verse from modern English translations; this refers to the plea for cleansing from "secret faults"</note>; yet he adds to this: *cleanse me from hidden faults.*

He knows when it is best for you to know that your sins are forgiven.

I Answer: Do not despise the accusations of your **conscience**; rather, let them humble you all the more and keep you strictly to your duty; yet know that the **conscience** is but an under-servant and **God's deputy** <note>original: "Gedeputeerde" — an official representative or delegate acting on behalf of a higher authority</note>, and that it must accuse according to the **Law** if it accuses rightly. And thus the soul should cause the accusations of the **conscience** to cease, and answer with this: that it has fled to **Christ**, the only **Mediator** and **Surety** <note>original: "Borge" — a legal term for one who takes on another's debt</note>, and has cast this burden upon Him, and leans only on His merits, and has placed the sins in His hand as its **Advocate** and **Intercessor** with the **Father**; and that the **Gospel** requires no more of it.

And if the **conscience** should say: "That faith and conversion are imperfect and deficient, and that the guilt is increased rather than taken away by them," then he must answer again: "It is true; but I have dealt with the guilt of my faith and repentance just as I did with the others; I have taken it all to **Christ** and left it all to Him, and in this alone I rest. I expect no forgiveness on account of my imperfect faith and repentance—indeed, I would not wish to expect forgiveness for my sins because of my faith and conversion, even if they were ever so perfect—but only in and through **Jesus Christ**, the only **Surety**, **Redeemer**, and **Advocate**."

But furthermore, this **deputy** should be brought before his **Master**, who alone can command him to be silent; that is to say, the believer should go to **Christ** with the accusing **conscience** and request of Him that He command it to be silent, so that he might have peace of **conscience** and freedom from those accusations, which fall bitter and heavy.

## CHAPTER IX.

### How to use *Christ* to cleanse us from our daily stains.

Having spoken of using **Christ** to ward off the guilt of our **daily transgressions**, we now proceed to speak of the manner of using **Christ** for the removal of the **filth** <note>original: "vuiligheidt" — referring to the moral pollution or defilement of sin rather than its legal guilt</note> that clings to the soul through **daily transgressions**.

For every sin defiles a person. *Matthew 15:20.* and even the best are said to have their spots, and to stand in need of washing, which presupposes filth and contagion. *Ephesians 5:27; John 13:8, 10.* Therefore we are so often called to this duty of washing and cleansing ourselves. *Isaiah 1:16; Jeremiah 4:14; Acts 22:16* <note>The original text cites verse 17, but the context of washing away sins is found in verse 16</note>. **David** prays for his washing. *Psalm 51:4, 9.* And it is **Christ’s** work to wash. *1 Corinthians 6:11; Revelation 1:5; Ephesians 5:26;* see *Titus 3:5.* Now, to speak of this, we shall maintain the same **method** <note>original: "Methode" — a systematic way of teaching or instruction</note>, and show **first**, what **Christ** has done to take away this filth; and **secondly**, in what manner we must use Him for this end, so that our stains and filth may be removed, in order that we may be holy.

Regarding the first: **Christ** has done these things to purge out the filth of our daily failings and transgressions.

## Questions, or Objections
->answered.<-

But alas! some might object / and say / even our **Faith** / which must bring the rest of our filthiness to the **Fountain of Christ’s Blood** / is defiled / how then can we expect / to be made clean? I answer. The **Blood of Jesus Christ** is sufficiently powerful / to wash away all our filthiness / the filthiness of **Faith** as well as of other deeds. Therefore, when **Faith** / like a hand <note>The image of faith as a "hand" that reaches out to receive Christ's grace was a common teaching in 17th-century Protestant theology.</note> / carries the filthiness of the **Soul** away to **Christ** / to be washed in his **Blood** / then let that dirty hand go along with the dirt that is in it; give **Christ** the **Faith** and everything to be washed.

Secondly. But what shall I do / if my **Conscience** / notwithstanding all this, shall continually accuse me of uncleanness / and cry out against me as filthy and abominable? I answer. Take the same along with you to the **Blood of Jesus** / so that it might be purified thereby / Heb. 9: v. 14. And here alone shall we get our hearts sprinkled for the purification of an evil **Conscience** / Heb. 10: v. 22. The **Conscience** must be baptized (so to speak) in the **Blood of Jesus** / and so it shall be pure; and taking our filthy **Hearts** to this purifying **Fountain** to be washed / so shall we get them delivered and cleansed from an evil **Conscience** / so that it shall no longer have ground for accusation against us. If we can say / that we have placed our filthy **Souls** in the hands of the great **Purifier Jesus Christ** / and have brought all our contaminations to his **Blood** / what then can the **Conscience** say against us? It is true / the **Lord** may permit / that our **Conscience** still barks <note>original: *bast*; a vivid metaphor comparing a guilty conscience to a barking dog that refuses to be silenced.</note> against us / and [shows] our filthiness to us

# Christ the Truth,

3. The Fourth general matter, which is remarkable here / is / that he is not only called *Truth*, but the *Truth*, just as he is the *Way*, and the *Life*; and not only *Truthful*, but *Truth* in the abstract <note>To be "Truth in the abstract" means that he is the very essence of Truth itself, rather than merely someone who happens to tell the truth.</note> / which signifies:

1. That he is in every way the *Truth* / however we consider him / whether as *God* / or as *Mediator*.
2. That all *truth* is in him / all *truth* of *salvation* for us is to be found in him.
3. That all that is in him / is *truth* / his *Natures* <note>Theologians of this period focused on the "two natures" of Christ—his being simultaneously fully God and fully man.</note> / *Offices* <note>The "Threefold Office" refers to Christ's roles as Prophet, Priest, and King.</note> / *Actions* / *Words* / *Works* / &c. are all *truthful*.
4. That he is *pure* and *unmixed* *Truth*; no *lie* is in him / no *error* / or *mistake* is there.
5. That the *Truth* in him is in its *perfection* and *excellence*; in even the *truest* of *Men* it is very *imperfect*.

O what an *Excellent One* he must be! how perfectly made fit / and provided for us! Oh that our *Souls* could love him / and embrace him / and rest upon him as *all-sufficient*!

...be for us all to take hold of and grasp Him who is the *Truth*, and the *Truth* alone? Seeing that:

1. All other ways that we might take will eventually be found to be a lie.
2. He is the substance <note>original: *weesen*; referring to actual reality as opposed to a mere shadow</note>, and no shadow, and all those who love Him shall inherit that which is enduring and essential: For He shall fill their treasuries, *Proverbs 8: verse 21*.
3. Those who embrace Him shall not wander off, nor be misled: For His mouth shall speak the truth, and wickedness is an abomination to His lips, *Proverbs 8: verse 7*. 4. He shall make good all His promises in His own time, and give existence and substance to them all: For He is the *Truth*, and the *truth* must stand by His promises and fulfill them all.
5. He shall never, no never, forsake His own, nor abandon them, *Hebrews 13: verse 5*. First, that he ought not to rest in whatever measure of knowledge he has obtained, or can obtain here, as if he had enough and did not need to labor for more; but he should always take his duty to heart, to seek and strive for more.

Second. Whenever he is engaged with any <term>means</term> <note>Referring back to the "means of grace" mentioned on the previous page, such as communal worship or private study.</note> of knowledge—such as preaching, reading, conversing, etc.—his heart should be focused on Christ alone. He ought to hang upon His lips for a word of instruction, and look out with <term>eagerness</term> <note>original: "gretigheidt"—in this context, an earnest, holy longing for spiritual food.</note> for a word from His mouth; he should send many a <term>post</term> <note>original: "post"—a 17th-century metaphor for sending urgent prayers to heaven like couriers or messengers.</note> to Heaven, many shooting desires for light and understanding, and do so with simplicity and sincerity, and not for wicked ends or out of hypocrisy.

Third, let him not think that there is no growth in knowledge simply because he does not easily notice it, or because he is not satisfied with the measure of it. Indeed, even if he notices more ignorance than he ever did before: if he grows in the knowledge of his own ignorance, that is a growth in knowledge that is not to be despised. In a certain way, what else can we know of God except that He far exceeds all our knowledge, and that He is an <term>Incomprehensible One</term> <note>A theological term for God's nature being beyond the full grasp of the human mind.</note> in all His ways.

Fourth, let him not think there is no growth in knowledge because he does not notice growth in this or that particular matter which he most desires. For if there is growth in the knowledge of other particulars that are necessary to be known, then there is no reason to complain. If a person does not grow, as he believes, in the knowledge of God and of the mysteries of the Gospel, yet if he grows in the discovery of the deceitfulness and wickedness of his own heart, he cannot say that he is not growing in knowledge.

->Truth, in a Time of Errors.<-

## CHAPTER XVI.

### How to use Christ as the *Truth*, when error prevails, and the spirit of error carries many away.

There is a time when the spirit of error goes forth, and the Truth is called into question, and many are led away by deceptions. For Satan can transform himself into an Angel of Light <note>original: *Engel des Lichts*; a reference to 2 Corinthians 11:14, describing how deception often wears the mask of holiness</note>, and create many great and fair-seeming pretenses of holiness, and introduce falsehoods to people under that pretext, and win the consent of many to the same. So it is that many, in such a time of temptation, lose their footing <note>original: *haar voeten uit-schieten*, literally "shoot out their feet," an idiom for slipping or falling into sin/error</note> and are brought to deviate from the right ways of God, embracing error and deceptions in place of truth. Now the question is: how shall a poor believer use Christ, who is the Truth, to keep themselves steadfast in the truth on such a day of trial <note>original: *beproeving*, meaning a period of testing or refining</note>, and not to embrace the way of error, however plausible and lovely it might seem to appear?

To satisfy this question, we shall propose these few things.

**Firstly**, In such a time when a spirit of error is let loose and rages, carrying several away, it would be good for all who wish to be held as upright and honest to walk in fear. It is not good to despise such a cunning and subtle enemy, especially in the "hour and power of darkness" <note>original: *uure en kracht der duysternis*; see Luke 22:53</note>. Then they are all called to take good heed, to stand upon their watchtower <note>original: *wacht-toorn*, a biblical metaphor for spiritual alertness, as in Habakkuk 2:1</note>, and to be jealous over their own corrupt hearts—which of themselves are sufficiently inclined to drink in error and accept temptation at all times, and much more so then.

**Fourthly**, to the end that they might be kept more wakeful and cautious, they must remember that it is a dishonorable thing for Christ that they should step aside in even the smallest matter of the truth; the denial of the smallest point of truth is, by consequence, a denial of Him who is the Truth itself. ## Warnings and directions.

For the further clearing of this matter, we shall point out some Warnings and further directions that are useful here; such as:

**First**, They must beware of thinking that God would come to them with Light and instruction in an extraordinary way, and reveal in some immediate manner the truth of the question in dispute: For this would be an open tempting and limiting of the Holy One of Israel. We must be satisfied with the means of instruction that he has appointed, and run to the *Law* and to the *testimony*; which are powerful to make a Man of God perfect, and fully equipped for all good works, 2 Tim. 3:16, 17, and to make us wise unto salvation, verse 15. There we must seek the Light, and there we must wait for him to breathe life into us by his Spirit, and to come with Light to show us the truth: For they are the *scripture of truth*, Dan. 10:21, and the *Law of the Lord, which is perfect, converting the Soul*, and *the commandment of the Lord, which is pure, enlightening the eyes*, etc. Psalm 19:7, 8. We have the ministry of the Word <term>Predikdienst: the formal office of preaching and the public teaching of the church</term>, which God has also instituted for this end, to make his mind known to us; there we must wait upon him and upon his Light. Thus we must wait at the posts of the doors of wisdom <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:34, depicting the seeker of truth as a beggar or student waiting outside the house of Wisdom.</note> and wait for the King of Light in his own way, in which he has placed us to wait
